title: Venn Diagrams
summary: Two question families: (1) region arithmetic — count union, intersection, only-regions, exactly-two, neither using inclusion-exclusion over labelled Venn regions; (2) relation selection — decide whether categories nest (definitional necessity), stay apart (impossibility) or intersect (possible but not forced). The arithmetic family is pure formula discipline; the relation family is two quick tests per pair. Label every region before computing and both become near-90% accuracy topics.

subtopics.title: What a Venn diagram encodes
subtopics.concept:
A Venn diagram is a picture of set membership: every point inside a circle belongs to that category; overlap regions belong to both. Two habits solve most CGL venn questions:

1. **Region bookkeeping.** Name the 4 regions of a two-circle diagram (only A, only B, both, neither) and the 8 regions of a three-circle one. Every question is a sum or difference of named regions.
2. **Relation reading.** 'Choose the right diagram for X, Y, Z' asks about *definitional* relations: is one category ALWAYS inside another (nested circles)? Can they NEVER meet (separate circles)? Otherwise (overlap possible but not forced) draw intersecting circles.

Draw the regions and label them with the given numbers before computing — unlabelled diagrams cause double-counting errors.

formulas.name: Two-set inclusion-exclusion
formulas.note: The intersection is counted twice on the right, so subtract once.

formulas.name: Only-regions
formulas.note: 'Only A' is A minus the overlap.

tricks.title: Label regions, don’t imagine them
tricks.body: Write the numbers INTO the regions: |A∩B| in the lens, only-A and only-B in the moons, neither outside. Sums become single looks instead of formula recalls.

example.q:
**Q.** 60 students; 35 like tea, 30 coffee, 10 both. How many like neither?

**Sol.** Tea-only 25 + both 10 + coffee-only 20 = 55 inside; 60 − 55 = **5**.
example.solution: Fill the diagram first; the answer is whatever region is left empty times its count.

mistakes: Counting the intersection twice when totalling.
Treating 'like tea' (including both) as 'like only tea'.
Forgetting the 'neither' region sits outside both circles.
subtopics.notes:
### What a Venn diagram shows
A Venn diagram is a picture of **membership**. Each circle is a group (people who drink tea, even numbers, doctors). A point inside a circle belongs to that group. A point where two circles overlap belongs to both. The rectangle around the circles is the **universal set** — everyone being talked about — and the space outside all circles holds those who belong to none.

The diagram is only useful if you read it by **regions**, not by circles. A region is a piece of the picture that cannot be split further by any circle line.

### Counting regions
- **Two** intersecting circles make **4** regions: only A, only B, both, neither.
- **Three** mutually intersecting circles make **8** regions: 3 "only" regions, 3 "exactly two" regions, 1 "all three" region and 1 "none" region.
- In general each region is a yes/no answer for every circle, so n circles drawn with every overlap give 2ⁿ regions (including the outside).
- Circle A alone is made of **4** of the 8 regions in a three-circle diagram: only A, A-and-B only, A-and-C only, and all three.

### Words → set symbols
| Phrase | Symbol | Regions (three circles) |
|---|---|---|
| in A or B (at least one) | A ∪ B | everything inside A or B |
| in both A and B | A ∩ B | A-B only **plus** all three |
| in A but not B | A − B | only A **plus** A-C only |
| in A and B but not C | (A ∩ B) − C | A-B only |
| in exactly one of A, B | (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B) | only A, only B |
| in none | outside all circles | the "none" region |

The commonest slip is to read "in both A and B" as the single A-and-B-only region. "Both A and B" says nothing about C, so the all-three region is included.

### Reading numbers off a diagram
When the numbers are written region by region, every question is just **adding the right regions**. Suppose a survey of news habits — Newspaper (N), TV (T), Radio (R) — gives: only N 20, only T 25, only R 5, N-T only 15, T-R only 6, N-R only 4, all three 10, none 15 (total 100).
- Total newspaper readers = 20 + 15 + 4 + 10 = **49** (all four N-regions).
- At least two sources = 15 + 6 + 4 + 10 = **35**.
- Exactly one source = 20 + 25 + 5 = **50**.
- Not TV = total − all T-regions = 100 − 56 = **44**.
- At most one source = exactly one + none = 50 + 15 = **65**.

### Negative phrases
- **Neither / none** is the outside region.
- **Not A** is everything outside circle A, including the none region.
- **At most one** includes those in no circle at all.
- **Either A or B but not both** is the two "only" regions.

### Method that never fails
1. Write the region numbers (or letters) in the picture.
2. Turn the phrase into a list of regions.
3. Add those regions only once each.

### Quick revision
- Read by regions; two circles = 4 regions, three circles = 8 (including outside).
- "Both A and B" includes the all-three region; "A and B only" does not.
- A − B keeps the parts of A outside B, whatever C does.
- Not A includes the none region; at most one = exactly one + none.
- List the regions first, then add each one once.

patterns.name: Phrase to set expression
patterns.howToSpot: A phrase like 'doctors and singers but not players' with options written in ∩, ∪ and − symbols.
patterns.logic:
1. List which regions the phrase covers.
2. For each option, list the regions it covers.
3. Pick the option whose regions match exactly.

*Why it works:* two expressions mean the same only if they cover the same regions.

example.q: Which expression shows 'in A and B but not C'?
example.solution: The phrase is the A-B-only region = **(A ∩ B) − C**. A ∩ B alone would also include the all-three region.

patterns.name: Reading region numbers
patterns.howToSpot: Numbers are given for each region (only A, A-B only, all three, none) and a question asks for a total.
patterns.logic:
1. Turn the question into a list of regions.
2. Add those region numbers, each once.
3. Use total − region sum for 'not' questions.

*Why it works:* regions never overlap, so adding them never double-counts.

example.q: Only N 20, N-T only 15, N-R only 4, all three 10. How many read the newspaper?

patterns.name: Counting regions
patterns.howToSpot: Asks how many regions a diagram has, or how many regions make up one circle.
patterns.logic:
1. Each region is a yes/no choice for every circle.
2. n circles with all overlaps → 2ⁿ regions including the outside.
3. Regions inside one circle of three = 2² = 4.

*Why it works:* every combination of in/out appears exactly once.

example.q: How many regions does a diagram of three mutually intersecting circles have (including the outside)?

patterns.name: Negative and 'at most' phrases
patterns.howToSpot: Phrases like not A, neither, at most one, either but not both.
patterns.logic:
1. 'Not A' = total − all regions of A (includes the none region).
2. 'At most one' = exactly one + none.
3. 'Either but not both' = the two only-regions.

*Why it works:* negative phrases are easiest as complements of positive ones.

example.q: Total 100; the four T-regions add to 56. How many do not watch TV?

subtopics.title: Two-circle counting
subtopics.concept:
With two sets there are exactly four regions: only A, only B, both, neither. Every two-circle question is a sum or difference of these:

- **Union** (at least one) = only A + only B + both.
- **Only A** = |A| − both; **Only B** = |B| − both.
- **Neither** = grand total − union.

Exam data typically gives |A|, |B| and the overlap (or hides one of them behind the union). Rearranging the inclusion-exclusion identity recovers any missing region in one step.

formulas.name: Two-set inclusion-exclusion
formulas.note: The intersection is counted twice on the right, so subtract once.

formulas.name: Only-regions
formulas.note: 'Only A' is A minus the overlap.

tricks.title: Label regions, don’t imagine them
tricks.body: Write the numbers INTO the regions: the lens, the two moons, and outside. Sums become single looks instead of formula recalls.

example.q:
**Q.** 60 students; 35 like tea, 30 coffee, 10 both. How many like neither?

**Sol.** Tea-only 25 + both 10 + coffee-only 20 = 55 inside; 60 − 55 = **5**.
example.solution: Fill the diagram first; the answer is whatever region is left, counted.

mistakes: Counting the intersection twice when totalling.
Treating 'like tea' (including both) as 'like only tea'.
Forgetting the 'neither' region sits outside both circles.
subtopics.notes:
### The four regions
Two overlapping circles A and B split the universe into four parts: **only A**, **only B**, **both**, **neither**. Every two-set question is a sum or a difference of these four numbers. Write them in the picture before doing anything else.

### Core formulas
- n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). The overlap is subtracted once because it was counted in both circles.
- Only A = n(A) − both; only B = n(B) − both.
- Exactly one = only A + only B = n(A) + n(B) − 2 × both.
- Neither = total − n(A ∪ B).
- Total = only A + only B + both + neither.

### Worked example
In a society of 150 families, 90 have a car, 70 have a two-wheeler and 40 have both.
- At least one = 90 + 70 − 40 = 120.
- Neither = 150 − 120 = **30**.
- Only car = 90 − 40 = 50; only two-wheeler = 70 − 40 = 30.
A common wrong answer is 70: taking only car + only two-wheeler = 80 and then 150 − 80, which forgets the 40 who have both.

### Reverse puzzles
Sometimes the question gives the answer regions and asks for a circle total or for the overlap. Use the same four boxes and fill in what you know.
- Given union and the two totals: both = n(A) + n(B) − union.
- If everybody is in at least one set: union = total, so both = n(A) + n(B) − total.
- Ratio clues: "only cricket is twice only football", with only C + only F = 30, gives only F = 10, only C = 20.

### Percentages
Treat the whole group as 100 and work in percent. Convert to people only at the end.
- 35% failed maths, 25% failed English, 10% failed both → failed at least one = 50%, so passed both = 50%. If 250 passed both, total = 250 ÷ 0.5 = 500.
- The trap: 100 − 35 − 25 = 40% "passed both" forgets that the 10% who failed both were subtracted twice.

### Maximum and minimum overlap
When the overlap is not given, it can move within limits (total N, sets of size a and b):
- **Maximum both** = the smaller set, min(a, b) — the small circle sits fully inside the big one.
- **Minimum both** = a + b − N, or 0 if that is negative — the circles overlap only as much as they are forced to.
- **Maximum neither** = N − max(a, b) — again when the smaller circle sits inside the larger.
- **Minimum neither** = N − (a + b), or 0 if negative.
Example: 60 students, 45 like tea, 35 like coffee → both is at least 45 + 35 − 60 = 20 and at most 35.

### Quick revision
- Four boxes: only A, only B, both, neither — fill them first.
- Union = A + B − both; neither = total − union; exactly one = A + B − 2 × both.
- Everyone in at least one set → both = A + B − total.
- Percent questions: work in %, convert at the end; passed both ≠ 100 − fail₁ − fail₂.
- Max both = smaller set; min both = A + B − N (not below 0); max neither = N − larger set.

patterns.name: Union and neither
patterns.howToSpot: Two totals, their overlap and the group size; asks at least one, neither or only one set.
patterns.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
patterns.logic:
1. Union = A + B − both.
2. Neither = total − union.
3. Only A = A − both.

*Why it works:* the overlap is counted twice in A + B, so it is removed once.

example.q: 150 families: 90 car, 70 two-wheeler, 40 both. How many have neither?

patterns.name: Reverse two-set puzzle
patterns.howToSpot: Some region values are given and a circle total, the overlap or the group size is asked; may include a ratio clue.
patterns.logic:
1. Draw the four boxes: only A, only B, both, neither.
2. Fill the known boxes.
3. Solve for the missing box from the total or the ratio.

*Why it works:* the four boxes always add to the total.

example.q: 30 like mango, 15 like only guava, 8 like neither. Group size?
example.solution: Mango (30, includes both) + only guava 15 + neither 8 = **53**.

patterns.name: Percentage sets
patterns.howToSpot: Data given in percent; the answer may be in percent or in people.
patterns.logic:
1. Work the whole problem in percent with total 100.
2. Find the percent of the asked region.
3. Convert: people = percent × total ÷ 100 (or total = people ÷ percent × 100).

*Why it works:* percentages obey the same region algebra as counts.

example.q: 35% failed maths, 25% failed English, 10% failed both; 250 passed both. Total?
example.solution: Failed at least one = 50%, passed both = 50% → total = **500**.

patterns.name: Maximum and minimum overlap
patterns.howToSpot: The overlap is not given; asks the largest or smallest possible both / neither.
patterns.formula: min both = max(0, A + B − N); max both = min(A, B)
patterns.logic:
1. Max both = smaller set.
2. Min both = A + B − N (0 if negative).
3. Max neither = N − larger set; min neither = N − (A + B) (0 if negative).

*Why it works:* the smaller circle can sit fully inside the larger, or the circles can be pushed apart until the total forces overlap.

example.q: 60 students; 45 tea, 35 coffee. Minimum who like both?

subtopics.title: Three-circle counting
subtopics.concept:
With three sets A, B, C the master formula is

|A∪B∪C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A∩B| − |B∩C| − |A∩C| + |A∩B∩C|.

Two derived region-counts appear constantly:

- **Exactly two** = (|A∩B| − all3) + (|B∩C| − all3) + (|A∩C| − all3): each pairwise figure includes the triple region, which must be stripped from both pairs it contaminates.
- **Exactly one** = union − exactly-two − all-three.

Exam data usually gives the seven numbers directly (three singles, three pairs, one triple); plug them into the 8 regions and add or subtract as asked.

formulas.name: Three-set union
formulas.note: Add singles, subtract pairs, re-add the triple.

formulas.name: Exactly two sets
formulas.note: Sum of the three pairwise figures minus three times the triple.

formulas.name: Exactly one set
formulas.note: Strip the multi-set members from the union.

tricks.title: Triple-strip subtraction
tricks.body: Whenever a question says 'exactly two', your reflex is: pairwise sums overcount the core by 3. Compute pairwise sums, subtract 3×(all three), done.

example.solution: 'Exactly' always means: subtract every richer region, as many times as it was counted.

mistakes: Using pairwise figures as 'exactly two' without stripping the triple region.
Sign slips on the +all-three term in the union formula.
Adding 'neither/none' into the union before subtracting from the grand total.
subtopics.notes:
### The eight regions
Three circles A, B, C give seven regions inside and one outside:
- **Only A, only B, only C** — exactly one set.
- **A-B only, B-C only, A-C only** — exactly two sets.
- **A-B-C** — all three.
- **None** — outside all circles.

Always fill the diagram **from the centre outwards**: all three first, then the exactly-two regions, then the only regions, then none.

### The master formula
n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(B∩C) − n(A∩C) + n(A∩B∩C)

Why the triple is added back: it is counted 3 times in the singles, removed 3 times in the pairs, so it would be lost without the last term.

### Region formulas
- A-B only = n(A∩B) − all three (and the same for the other two pairs).
- Only A = n(A) − n(A∩B) − n(A∩C) + all three.
- Exactly two = (sum of pairwise) − 3 × all three.
- At least two = (sum of pairwise) − 2 × all three.
- Exactly one = union − exactly two − all three.

### Worked example
In a club of 60 members, 30 play cricket (C), 25 football (F), 20 hockey (H); 10 play C and F, 8 play F and H, 7 play C and H, and 4 play all three.
- Centre: 4.
- Exactly two: C-F only 10 − 4 = 6; F-H only 8 − 4 = 4; C-H only 7 − 4 = 3.
- Only C = 30 − 6 − 3 − 4 = 17; only F = 25 − 6 − 4 − 4 = 11; only H = 20 − 4 − 3 − 4 = 9.
- Union = 17 + 11 + 9 + 6 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 54 (the formula gives 30 + 25 + 20 − 10 − 8 − 7 + 4 = 54 as well).
- None = 60 − 54 = **6**.
Forgetting the "+ 4" gives a union of 50 and a wrong answer of 10.

### Reverse questions
- **Find the triple** from the union: rearrange the master formula. With singles 25, 30, 20, pairs 10, 8, 7 and union 55: 75 − 25 + x = 55, so x = 5.
- **Exactly-counts to sum of circles**: if 60 people are in exactly one set, 30 in exactly two and 10 in all three, then n(A) + n(B) + n(C) = 60 + 2 × 30 + 3 × 10 = 150, because a person in two circles is counted twice.

### Percent data
When the three sets are given in percent, take the total as 100 and use the same formulas. If 50%, 40% and 30% like three kinds of songs, with pairs 20%, 15%, 10% and all three 5%, the union is 80% and **20%** like none. Convert to people only at the end.

### Checks that catch mistakes
- No region can be negative. If "only A" comes out negative, a number was misread.
- The seven inside regions must add up to the union.
- "At least two" is always greater than or equal to "exactly two".

### Quick revision
- Fill from the centre: triple → exactly-two → only → none.
- Union = ΣA − Σpairs + triple.
- Exactly two = Σpairs − 3 × triple; at least two = Σpairs − 2 × triple.
- Only A = A − AB − AC + triple.
- ΣA = exactly one + 2 × exactly two + 3 × all three.
- Check: no negative region; seven regions sum to the union.

patterns.name: Three-set union and none
patterns.howToSpot: Three totals, three pairwise overlaps and the triple; asks at least one or none.
patterns.logic:
1. Union = ΣA − Σpairs + triple.
2. None = total − union.
3. Check that no region is negative.

*Why it works:* the triple is added in 3 times and removed 3 times, so it is added back once.

example.q: 60 members: 30, 25, 20; pairs 10, 8, 7; all three 4. None?

patterns.name: Exactly one / exactly two / at least two
patterns.howToSpot: Asks how many belong to exactly one, exactly two or at least two sets.
patterns.logic:
1. Exactly two = Σpairs − 3 × triple.
2. At least two = Σpairs − 2 × triple.
3. Exactly one = union − exactly two − triple.

*Why it works:* each pairwise figure contains the triple once.

example.q: Pairs 15, 12, 10; triple 5. Exactly two?

patterns.name: Fill one region
patterns.howToSpot: Asks for one specific region: only A, or A-and-B-but-not-C.
patterns.logic:
1. A-B only = n(A∩B) − triple.
2. Only A = n(A) − n(A∩B) − n(A∩C) + triple.
3. Fill from the centre outwards if more regions are needed.

*Why it works:* subtracting both pairs removes the triple twice, so it is added back once.

example.q: n(A) = 45, n(A∩B) = 15, n(A∩C) = 12, triple 6. Only A?

patterns.name: Reverse three-set puzzle
patterns.howToSpot: The union or the exactly-counts are given and the triple or the circle sum is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Rearrange the master formula for the unknown term.
2. Or use ΣA = exactly one + 2 × exactly two + 3 × all three.
3. Verify by filling the eight regions.

*Why it works:* each person is counted once for every circle they are in.

example.q: Everyone in at least one of three sets; 60 in exactly one, 30 in exactly two, 100 people. Sum of the three circle totals?

subtopics.title: Choosing the correct diagram
subtopics.concept:
For 'Which diagram represents Doctors, Men, Writers?' style questions, decide each pair with two tests:

1. **Necessity test** — is every X definitionally a Y? (Every mother is a female.) → circle of X drawn **inside** Y.
2. **Impossibility test** — can X and Y never share a member? (A square and a triangle.) → **separate** circles.
3. Otherwise — overlap possible but neither forced (doctors and writers) → **intersecting** circles.

Same-type categories usually intersect; category-of-category pairs (squares/rectangles/polygons) nest; mutually exclusive definitions separate.

tricks.title: Test one pair at a time
tricks.body: Never judge the whole picture at once. Run necessity/impossibility on each pair; the correct option is the only one agreeing on every pair.

example.q:
**Q.** Mothers, Females, Engineers.

**Sol.** Mothers ⊂ Females (necessity). Engineers ∩ Females possible (female engineers) and Engineers ⊄ Females (male engineers) → intersecting. Match the option reflecting both facts.
example.solution: One wrong pair eliminates an option — work pair by pair until one option survives.

mistakes: Drawing engineers inside females because most examples in mind are female.
Missing a third category's relation to the nested pair.
subtopics.notes:
### What the question asks
You get three words (Doctors, Men, Writers; Even numbers, Odd numbers, Prime numbers) and must choose the circle picture that shows how the groups are related. There are no numbers — only **relationships**.

### Two tests for every pair
Look at the three pairs one at a time: (1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 3).
1. **Inside test.** Is every member of X *always* a member of Y? Every sparrow is a bird → the Sparrows circle is drawn **inside** Birds.
2. **Apart test.** Can X and Y *never* share a member? No number is both even and odd → the two circles are drawn **separate**.
3. If neither test holds, some members can be in both and some cannot → the circles **intersect**.

Judge by definition, not by what is usual. A doctor *can* be a woman and a woman *can* be a doctor, so Doctors and Women intersect.

### The shapes that appear
| Relationship | Picture | Example |
|---|---|---|
| X ⊂ Y ⊂ Z | three nested circles | Sparrows, Birds, Animals |
| X, Y separate, both inside Z | two separate circles inside a third | Pens, Pencils, Stationery |
| X, Y intersect, both inside Z | two intersecting circles inside a third | Even numbers, Multiples of 3, Integers |
| X ⊂ Y, Z apart from both | one inside another, third separate | Whales, Mammals, Fish |
| X ⊂ Y, Z crosses both | one inside another, third intersecting both | Fathers, Men, Doctors |
| X ⊂ Y, Z crosses only Y | third cuts the outer circle only | Natural numbers, Integers, Negative numbers |
| X, Y intersect, Z inside their overlap | third inside the common part | Multiples of 5, Multiples of 7, Multiples of 35 |
| X, Y separate, Z crosses both | two separate circles joined by a third | Even numbers, Odd numbers, Prime numbers |
| all pairs intersect | three intersecting circles | Teachers, Women, Singers |
| two intersect, third apart | two intersecting circles and a separate one | Women, Engineers, Rivers |
| no links | three separate circles | Pens, Rivers, Tigers |

### Tricky cases
- **Number sets** are exact: check a sample. 2 is even and prime, 3 is odd and prime, 9 is odd and not prime — so Primes cross both Even and Odd while Even and Odd never meet.
- **"Crosses only the outer circle."** Negative numbers include −1 (an integer) and −½ (not an integer), and no negative number is a natural number. So the Negative circle cuts Integers but stays away from the Naturals circle inside it.
- **Inside their overlap.** Every multiple of 35 is a multiple of both 5 and 7, so it sits inside the common part of those two circles.
- **Gender words.** Fathers ⊂ Men; Mothers ⊂ Women; Men and Women are separate.

### Method
1. Write the three pairs.
2. Mark each pair **inside**, **apart** or **cross**.
3. Match the three marks to the picture — do not jump to a picture from the first pair alone.

### Quick revision
- For each pair: always both → inside; never both → apart; else → cross.
- Judge by definition, not by what is common.
- Test number sets with small examples (2, 3, 9, −1, −½).
- A third circle can cross both, only the outer, or sit inside an overlap — check each pair separately.
- Decide all three pairs before picking the picture.

patterns.name: Nested chain
patterns.howToSpot: Each word is a type of the next: sparrow → bird → animal.
patterns.logic:
1. Check that every X is a Y and every Y is a Z.
2. Draw the circles one inside the next.

*Why it works:* subset of a subset is a subset.

example.q: Sparrows, Birds, Animals.
example.solution: Every sparrow is a bird, every bird an animal → **three nested circles**.

patterns.name: Subsets inside a bigger set
patterns.howToSpot: Two words are kinds of the third word.
patterns.logic:
1. Put both smaller groups inside the big circle.
2. Decide whether the two smaller groups can share members: never → separate; sometimes → intersecting.
3. If one group is inside another and the third is unrelated, draw the third apart.

*Why it works:* the relation between the two small groups is separate from their relation to the big one.

example.q: Pens, Pencils, Stationery.
example.solution: Both are stationery; nothing is both a pen and a pencil → **two separate circles inside a third**.

patterns.name: Partial overlaps
patterns.howToSpot: No word is a kind of another; some pairs can share members, some cannot.
patterns.logic:
1. Test each pair: can share → intersect; never → apart.
2. All three share → three intersecting circles.
3. Two share and the third is unrelated → two intersecting circles plus a separate one.

*Why it works:* with no subsets, only the cross/apart choice matters for each pair.

example.q: Teachers, Women, Singers.
example.solution: Every pair can share members → **three circles, each pair intersecting**.

patterns.name: Mixed: inside plus crossing
patterns.howToSpot: One word is a kind of another and the third cuts across, or one sits inside the overlap of two.
patterns.logic:
1. Draw the subset pair first.
2. Test the third word against the inner and the outer circle separately.
3. If the third word is a subset of two overlapping sets, place it inside their common part.

*Why it works:* the third circle's relation to the inner circle can differ from its relation to the outer one.

example.q: Fathers, Men, Doctors.
example.solution: Fathers ⊂ Men; a doctor can be a father or a man → **one inside another, third intersecting both**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two totals and the overlap; asks at least one, only one or neither.
pyqPatterns.approach: Union = A + B − both; neither = total − union; only A = A − both.

example.q: In a class of 60, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 10 like both. How many like neither?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Some regions are given; the overlap, a circle total or the group size is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Draw four boxes (only A, only B, both, neither), fill the known ones and solve for the gap.

example.q: Everyone in a class of 80 plays chess or carrom; 50 play chess and 40 carrom. How many play both?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Data in percent, answer in percent or in people.
pyqPatterns.approach: Solve in percent with total 100, convert to people at the end.

example.q: 70% watch cricket, 60% football, 40% both. What percent watch neither?
example.solution: Union 90% → neither **10%**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Overlap not given; asks its largest or smallest possible value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Max both = smaller set; min both = A + B − N (not below 0); max neither = N − larger set.

example.q: 80 people; 50 like cricket, 40 hockey. Maximum who like neither?
example.solution: Hockey inside cricket → neither = 80 − 50 = **30**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three totals, three pairs, the triple and a group size.
pyqPatterns.approach: Union = ΣA − Σpairs + triple; none = total − union.

example.q: 200 people: coffee 90, tea 80, milk 70; pairs 40, 35, 30; all three 15. How many drink none?
example.solution: Union 150 → none **50**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Asks for exactly one, exactly two or at least two sets.
pyqPatterns.approach: Exactly two = Σpairs − 3 × triple; at least two = Σpairs − 2 × triple; exactly one = union − exactly two − triple.

example.q: Pairs 8, 7, 6 and all three 3. Exactly two?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Numbers are written in each region; the question describes a group in words.
pyqPatterns.approach: List the regions the phrase covers and add them once each; use total − regions for 'not' phrases.

example.q: Only N 20, only T 25, only R 5, N-T 15, T-R 6, N-R 4, all 10. How many use exactly one source?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three words; options describe circle pictures.
pyqPatterns.approach: For each pair decide inside / apart / cross by definition, then match all three marks to one picture.

example.q: Even numbers, Odd numbers, Prime numbers.
example.solution: Even and odd never meet; 2 and 3 are prime → **two separate circles, with the third intersecting both**.

solvedExamples.q: In a class of **60 students, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 10 like both.** How many students like **neither** tea nor coffee?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add both counts, subtract the overlap once, subtract from the total.

solvedExamples.q: In a survey, **8 people read A and B, 7 read B and C, 6 read A and C, and 3 read all three.** How many read **exactly two** papers?
solvedExamples.solution: (8 − 3) + (7 − 3) + (6 − 3) = **12**. Each pairwise figure wrongly includes the triple readers.

solvedExamples.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Doctors, Men and Writers**?
options: Three completely separate circles
Doctors and Writers both inside the Men circle
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Doctors inside Men; Writers a separate circle
solvedExamples.solution: No category is definitionally inside another (a doctor need not be a man; men need not write), and none is impossible to combine. So all three circles pairwise intersect.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Run necessity (nesting) and impossibility (separation) tests pair by pair; neither applies here.

solvedExamples.q: Of **200 people, 90 drink coffee, 80 tea, 70 milk; 40 coffee and tea, 35 tea and milk, 30 coffee and milk; 15 all three.** How many drink **none**?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add singles, subtract pairs, re-add triple, subtract from total.

practice.q: In a group, **|A ∪ B| = 40**, the number of elements in **A only is 15** and in **B only is 12**. How many elements are in **both A and B**?
practice.solution: Union = only-A + only-B + both → 40 = 15 + 12 + both → both = **13**.
practice.shortcut: The three inside-regions sum to the union.

practice.q: In a school, **40 students play hockey, 25 play cricket and 12 play both.** How many students play **hockey or cricket** (at least one)?
practice.shortcut: Singles minus overlap.

practice.q: In a survey, **70% of people watch cricket, 60% watch football and 40% watch both.** What percentage watch **neither**?
practice.shortcut: Percentages behave exactly like counts — total is 100.

practice.q: In a class of **80 students, every student plays at least one of chess and carrom. 50 play chess and 40 play carrom.** How many play **both**?
practice.solution: At least one = 80 → 50 + 40 − both = 80 → both = **10**.
practice.shortcut: 'Everyone plays' pins the union equal to the class strength.
Sum, subtract pairs, re-add the triple.

practice.q: In a colony of newspaper readers, **45 people read the Herald, 25 read both the Herald and the Tribune.** How many read **only the Herald**?
practice.solution: Only Herald = 45 − 25 = **20**.
practice.shortcut: 'Only X' = X minus the overlap.

practice.q: A club's three sports sections show: **15 members in badminton only, 10 in tennis only, 8 in chess only, 6 in badminton and tennis only, 5 in tennis and chess only, 4 in badminton and chess only, and 2 in all three.** How many members play **at least one** of the three sports?
practice.solution: The seven regions are disjoint — add them: 15+10+8+6+5+4+2 = **50**.
practice.shortcut: When every region is given 'only'-style, no formula — just add.

practice.q: Given **|A| = 22, |B| = 19, |C| = 17, |A∩B| = 9, |B∩C| = 7, |A∩C| = 6, |A∩B∩C| = 4** — how many elements belong to **exactly one** set?
practice.solution: Exactly two = (9−4)+(7−4)+(6−4) = 10. Exactly one = union − exactly two − triple = 40 − 10 − 4 = **26**.
practice.shortcut: Union minus everyone in two or three sets.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Squares, Rectangles and Polygons**?
options: Squares inside Rectangles, both inside Polygons
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Squares and Rectangles intersecting, both inside Polygons
Three completely separate circles
practice.solution: Every square is a rectangle and every rectangle is a polygon — a fully nested chain of circles.
practice.shortcut: Necessity test passes for every pair → nested circles.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Mothers, Females and Engineers**?
options: Mothers and Engineers inside Females
Engineers inside Females; Mothers separate
Mothers inside Females; Engineers circle intersecting both
All three circles intersecting equally
practice.solution: Every mother is definitionally a female → Mothers inside Females. Engineers can be male or female and may or may not be mothers → the Engineers circle crosses both.
practice.shortcut: Definition decides nesting; possibility decides intersection.

practice.q: **|A ∩ B| = 8, |A − B| = 10, |B| = 20 and 7 elements belong to neither set.** What is the size of the **universal set** (all elements considered)?
practice.shortcut: Four disjoint regions: both, A-only, B-only, neither.

practice.q: **|A| = 25, |B| = 20 and |A ∩ B| = 8.** How many elements are in **exactly one** of A and B?
practice.shortcut: Strip the lens from each circle and add the moons.

practice.q: In a batch of **120 trainees: 55 know Python, 45 know Java, 40 know C++; 20 know Python and Java, 18 know Java and C++, 15 know Python and C++; 8 know all three.** How many trainees know **none** of the three?
practice.shortcut: Full inclusion-exclusion, then subtract from the batch.

practice.q: **|A∩B| = 12, |B∩C| = 10, |A∩C| = 9 and |A∩B∩C| = 5.** How many elements belong to **at least two** of the sets?
practice.solution: At least two = exactly two + all three = (12−5)+(10−5)+(9−5) + 5 = 7+5+4+5 = **21**. Shortcut: pairwise sum 31 counts the triple 3 times → 31 − 2×5 = 21.
practice.shortcut: Pairwise sum − 2 × triple = at-least-two.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Words, English words and Hindi words**?
options: Three circles, each pair intersecting
English words inside Words; Hindi words a separate circle outside
All three nested inside one another
English and Hindi circles inside Words, not overlapping each other
practice.solution: Both are subsets of Words (necessity), and a word cannot be English and Hindi at once (impossibility) → two disjoint circles inside the big one.
practice.shortcut: One pair needs the impossibility test — the other two are simple nestings.

practice.q: In a three-circle diagram of Doctors (D), Singers (S) and Players (P), which expression shows the people who are **doctors and singers but not players**?
options: D ∩ S ∩ P
(D ∩ S) − P
D ∩ S
(D ∪ S) − P
practice.solution: The phrase needs D and S together, with P removed: **(D ∩ S) − P**, the single D-S-only region. D ∩ S alone also contains the all-three region; D ∩ S ∩ P is only the all-three region; (D ∪ S) − P also includes people who are only doctors or only singers.
practice.shortcut: 'And' → ∩, 'but not' → −. Check whether the all-three region sneaks in.

practice.q: Which expression shows the elements that belong to **exactly one of A and B**?
options: A ∪ B
A − B
A ∩ B
practice.solution: Exactly one = in A or B, but not in both: **(A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B)**, which is only A + only B. A ∪ B also includes the overlap; A ∩ B is the overlap itself; A − B misses the only-B part.
practice.shortcut: Exactly one = union minus overlap.

practice.q: Which expression shows the elements that are **in C but in neither A nor B**?
options: C − (A ∩ B)
C − A
C − (A ∪ B)
(A ∪ B) − C
practice.solution: 'Neither A nor B' means outside A **and** outside B, i.e. outside A ∪ B. So the set is **C − (A ∪ B)** = only C. C − (A ∩ B) wrongly keeps C-elements that are in just one of A, B; C − A still keeps the B-C-only region; (A ∪ B) − C is the opposite region.
practice.shortcut: Neither A nor B = remove the union, not the overlap.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people use **at least two** of the three sources?
practice.solution: At least two = the three exactly-two regions + all three = 15 + 6 + 4 + 10 = **35**. 25 misses the all-three region; 45 wrongly adds the 'none' group.
practice.shortcut: At least two = exactly-two regions + centre.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people **read the newspaper** (with or without other sources)?
practice.solution: All four regions inside N: only N 20 + N-T 15 + N-R 4 + all three 10 = **49**. 20 is only-N; 39 forgets the all-three region.
practice.shortcut: A whole circle = its 4 regions.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people use the **newspaper or the radio but not TV**?
practice.solution: Regions in N or R and outside T: only N 20 + only R 5 + N-R only 4 = **29**. 25 forgets the N-R region; 39 wrongly adds the all-three region, which contains TV watchers.
practice.shortcut: Remove every region that touches T.

practice.q: Three circles are drawn so that every pair overlaps and there is a region common to all three. Counting the space outside all circles, how many separate **regions** does the diagram have?
practice.solution: Each region is a yes/no choice for each circle: 2 × 2 × 2 = **8** (7 inside the circles + 1 outside). 7 forgets the outside region.
practice.shortcut: n circles → 2ⁿ regions including outside.

practice.q: In a standard diagram of three mutually intersecting circles A, B and C, **how many regions** together make up circle A?
practice.solution: Circle A is split by B and C into: only A, A-B only, A-C only and all three = **4** regions. 1 is only A; 3 forgets the centre.
practice.shortcut: A region inside A is a yes/no choice for B and C: 2 × 2 = 4.

practice.q: Two intersecting circles are drawn inside a rectangle that stands for the universal set. How many separate **regions** does the picture have?
practice.solution: Only A, only B, both, and the part of the rectangle outside both circles = **4**. 3 forgets the outside region.
practice.shortcut: Two circles → 2² = 4 regions.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people use **exactly one** source?
practice.solution: Exactly one = only N + only T + only R = 20 + 25 + 5 = **50**. 65 wrongly adds the 15 who use none; 35 is the at-least-two count.
practice.shortcut: Exactly one = the three 'only' regions.

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people **do not watch TV**?
practice.solution: TV regions = 25 + 15 + 6 + 10 = 56, so not TV = 100 − 56 = **44**. 75 subtracts only the 'only T' region; 29 forgets the 15 who use nothing.
practice.shortcut: Not T = total − whole T circle (the none group stays in).

practice.q:
A survey of **100 people** on how they get news — Newspaper (N), TV (T) and Radio (R) — gave these region counts:

- Only N: 20 · Only T: 25 · Only R: 5
- N and T only: 15 · T and R only: 6 · N and R only: 4
- All three: 10 · None of the three: 15

How many people use **at most one** of the three sources?
practice.solution: At most one = exactly one + none = 50 + 15 = **65**. 50 forgets that zero sources is also 'at most one'; 35 is the at-least-two count.
practice.shortcut: At most one = total − at least two = 100 − 35.

practice.q: In a housing society of **150 families, 90 have a car, 70 have a two-wheeler and 40 have both**. How many families have **neither**?
practice.solution: At least one = 90 + 70 − 40 = 120. Neither = 150 − 120 = **30**. 70 comes from 150 − (50 + 30), which forgets the 40 families who have both.
practice.shortcut: Neither = total − (A + B − both).

practice.q: Of **250 employees, 140 speak Hindi, 120 speak Telugu and 30 speak neither**. How many speak **only Telugu**?
practice.solution: At least one = 250 − 30 = 220. Both = 140 + 120 − 220 = 40. Only Telugu = 120 − 40 = **80**. 40 is the 'both' figure; 100 is only Hindi.
practice.shortcut: Find both first, then subtract it from the circle.

practice.q: In a group, **30 people like mango, 15 like only guava, 12 like both mango and guava, and 8 like neither**. How many people are in the group?
practice.solution: The 30 mango-lovers already include the 12 who like both. Group = mango 30 + only guava 15 + neither 8 = **53**. 65 adds the 12 a second time.
practice.shortcut: Check whether a given figure is a whole circle or an 'only' region.

practice.q: In a class of **46 students, 10 play both cricket and football and 6 play neither**. The number who play **only cricket is twice** the number who play only football. How many play **cricket**?
practice.solution: Only C + only F = 46 − 6 − 10 = 30, with only C = 2 × only F → only F = 10, only C = 20. Cricket = only C + both = 20 + 10 = **30**. 20 is only cricket.
practice.shortcut: Fill the four boxes; the ratio splits the 'only' total.

practice.q: In a town, **65% of adults read a Hindi paper, 40% read an English paper and 20% read both**. If **3,000 adults read neither**, how many adults are there in the town?
practice.shortcut: Find the percent of the known group, then scale up.

practice.q: In an examination, **35% of candidates failed in Mathematics, 25% failed in English and 10% failed in both**. If **250 candidates passed in both** subjects, how many candidates appeared?
practice.solution: Failed at least one = 35 + 25 − 10 = 50%, so passed both = 50%. Total = 250 × 100 ÷ 50 = **500**. 625 comes from 100 − 35 − 25 = 40%, which forgets to add back the 10% who failed both.
practice.shortcut: Passed both = 100 − (fail₁ + fail₂ − fail both).

practice.q: In a class of **60 students, 45 like tea and 35 like coffee**. What is the **minimum** number of students who like both?
practice.solution: The circles can be pushed apart only until they fill the class: 45 + 35 − 60 = **20** must overlap. 35 is the *maximum* (coffee fully inside tea); 0 is impossible because 45 + 35 > 60.
practice.shortcut: Min both = A + B − N (not below 0).

practice.q: In a group of **80 people, 50 like cricket and 40 like hockey**. What is the **maximum** number of people who like **neither** game?
practice.solution: Neither is largest when the circles cover as few people as possible — hockey fully inside cricket. Then at least one = 50 and neither = 80 − 50 = **30**. 0 is the minimum; 10 is the minimum overlap.
practice.shortcut: Max neither = N − larger set.

practice.q: A sports club has **60 members: 30 play cricket, 25 play football and 20 play hockey; 10 play cricket and football, 8 play football and hockey, 7 play cricket and hockey, and 4 play all three**. How many members play **none** of the three?
practice.solution: Union = 30 + 25 + 20 − 10 − 8 − 7 + 4 = 54. None = 60 − 54 = **6**. 10 comes from forgetting to add back the 4 who play all three.
practice.shortcut: Union = ΣA − Σpairs + triple.

practice.q: In a survey, **50% of people like Hindi songs, 40% like Tamil songs and 30% like Punjabi songs; 20% like Hindi and Tamil, 15% like Tamil and Punjabi, 10% like Hindi and Punjabi, and 5% like all three**. What percentage like **none** of the three?
practice.shortcut: Percent data works exactly like counts.

practice.q: For three sets, **|A ∩ B| = 15, |B ∩ C| = 12, |A ∩ C| = 10 and |A ∩ B ∩ C| = 5**. How many elements belong to **exactly two** of the sets?
practice.solution: Each pairwise figure contains the triple once: (15 − 5) + (12 − 5) + (10 − 5) = 10 + 7 + 5 = **22**. 37 is the raw pairwise sum; 27 is 'at least two' (22 + 5).
practice.shortcut: Exactly two = Σpairs − 3 × triple.

practice.q: In a school club of **70 students, 30 take Music, 28 take Dance and 25 take Drama; 12 take Music and Dance, 10 take Dance and Drama, 9 take Music and Drama, and 4 take all three**. How many take **exactly one** activity?
practice.solution: Only Music = 30 − 12 − 9 + 4 = 13; only Dance = 28 − 12 − 10 + 4 = 10; only Drama = 25 − 10 − 9 + 4 = 10. Exactly one = **33**. 56 is the union; 19 is exactly two.
practice.shortcut: Exactly one = union − exactly two − triple = 56 − 19 − 4.

practice.q: For three sets, **|A| = 45, |A ∩ B| = 15, |A ∩ C| = 12 and |A ∩ B ∩ C| = 6**. How many elements are in **only A**?
practice.solution: Only A = 45 − 15 − 12 + 6 = **24**. Subtracting both pairs removes the triple twice, so it is added back once; 18 forgets that.
practice.shortcut: Only A = A − AB − AC + ABC.

practice.q: In an office, **40 people speak Kannada; 18 speak Kannada and Hindi, 15 speak Kannada and Tamil, and 7 speak all three languages**. How many speak **only Kannada**?
practice.solution: Only Kannada = 40 − 18 − 15 + 7 = **14**. 7 forgets to add back the 7 who were subtracted twice; 22 subtracts only the Hindi overlap.
practice.shortcut: Subtract both pairs, add the triple back once.

practice.q: For three sets, **|A| = 25, |B| = 30, |C| = 20, |A ∩ B| = 10, |B ∩ C| = 8, |A ∩ C| = 7** and **|A ∪ B ∪ C| = 55**. How many elements are in **all three** sets?
practice.solution: 55 = 25 + 30 + 20 − 10 − 8 − 7 + x = 50 + x → x = **5**. Check: only A = 13, only B = 17, only C = 10 — no region is negative.
practice.shortcut: Rearrange the master formula for the missing term.

practice.q: Each of **100 people reads at least one of three magazines. 60 read exactly one and 30 read exactly two**. What is the **sum of the readerships** of the three magazines?
practice.solution: All three = 100 − 60 − 30 = 10. A reader of two magazines is counted twice and a reader of three is counted three times: 60 + 2 × 30 + 3 × 10 = **150**. 100 counts each person once.
practice.shortcut: ΣA = exactly one + 2 × exactly two + 3 × all three.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Natural numbers, Whole numbers and Integers**?
options: Two separate circles inside a third circle
Three circles, each pair intersecting
One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
Three nested circles, one inside the next
practice.solution: Every natural number (1, 2, 3, …) is a whole number, and every whole number (0, 1, 2, …) is an integer → **three nested circles**.
practice.shortcut: Each word is a type of the next → nested.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Sparrows, Birds and Animals**?
options: Three nested circles, one inside the next
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Two separate circles inside a third circle
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
practice.solution: Every sparrow is a bird and every bird is an animal → **three nested circles**.
practice.shortcut: Type of a type → nested chain.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Pens, Pencils and Stationery**?
options: Three nested circles, one inside the next
Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
Three completely separate circles
Two separate circles inside a third circle
practice.solution: Pens and pencils are both stationery, but nothing is both a pen and a pencil → **two separate circles inside a third**.
practice.shortcut: Two kinds of one thing that cannot overlap.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Whales, Mammals and Fish**?
options: One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
Two separate circles inside a third circle
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
Three nested circles, one inside the next
practice.solution: Every whale is a mammal. No fish is a mammal, so fish share nothing with mammals or whales → **one circle inside a second; the third separate from both**.
practice.shortcut: Test the third word against both circles.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Even numbers, Multiples of 3 and Integers**?
options: Two separate circles inside a third circle
Two intersecting circles, with the third inside their common part
Three nested circles, one inside the next
Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
practice.solution: Both are sets of integers. 6 is even and a multiple of 3, 4 is only even, 9 is only a multiple of 3 → they intersect. So **two intersecting circles inside a third**.
practice.shortcut: Two subsets of the big set — check whether they share members (6 does).

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Teachers, Women and Singers**?
options: One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Three completely separate circles
Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
practice.solution: A teacher may or may not be a woman or a singer, and a woman may or may not sing; all three can meet in one person → **three circles, each pair intersecting**.
practice.shortcut: No word is a type of another and every pair can share → all intersect.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Women, Engineers and Rivers**?
options: Three completely separate circles
Three circles, each pair intersecting
Two separate circles, with the third intersecting both
Two intersecting circles and a third separate circle
practice.solution: Some women are engineers → those two intersect. A river is neither a woman nor an engineer → **two intersecting circles and a third separate circle**.
practice.shortcut: Decide each pair; a non-person category stands apart.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Even numbers, Odd numbers and Prime numbers**?
options: Two separate circles inside a third circle
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
Two separate circles, with the third intersecting both
Three circles, each pair intersecting
practice.solution: No number is both even and odd → separate. 2 is even and prime, 3 is odd and prime, while 4 and 9 are not prime → the Prime circle cuts both. Answer: **two separate circles, with the third intersecting both**.
practice.shortcut: Test with 2, 3, 4, 9.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Fathers, Men and Doctors**?
options: Three circles, each pair intersecting
One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting only the outer circle
practice.solution: Every father is a man → Fathers inside Men. Some fathers are doctors and some are not; some men are doctors → the Doctors circle crosses both. Answer: **one circle inside a second; the third intersecting both**.
practice.shortcut: Draw the subset first, then test the third word against inner and outer.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Multiples of 4, Multiples of 2 and Multiples of 3**?
options: One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
Two intersecting circles, with the third inside their common part
practice.solution: Every multiple of 4 is a multiple of 2 → inside. 12 is a multiple of 4 (and 2) and of 3; 6 is a multiple of 2 and 3 but not 4; 9 is a multiple of 3 only → the third circle crosses both. Answer: **one circle inside a second; the third intersecting both**.
practice.shortcut: Check 12, 6 and 9.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Multiples of 5, Multiples of 7 and Multiples of 35**?
options: Two intersecting circles inside a third circle
Three nested circles, one inside the next
Two separate circles, with the third intersecting both
Two intersecting circles, with the third inside their common part
practice.solution: 35 = 5 × 7, so every multiple of 35 is a multiple of both 5 and 7. Multiples of 5 and 7 overlap (35, 70) but neither contains the other (10, 14). Answer: **two intersecting circles, with the third inside their common part**.
practice.shortcut: A common multiple sits in the overlap.

practice.q: Which diagram correctly represents **Natural numbers, Integers and Negative numbers**?
options: One circle inside a second; the third separate from both
Two separate circles, with the third intersecting both
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting only the outer circle
One circle inside a second; the third intersecting both
practice.solution: Every natural number is an integer → inside. −1 is a negative integer, but −½ is negative and not an integer → Negative numbers cut Integers. No natural number is negative → it stays away from the inner circle. Answer: **one circle inside a second; the third intersecting only the outer circle**.
practice.shortcut: Test −1 and −½; the third circle can touch the outer circle only.
